subtitle: What does the DHS Equity Policy ask of you as a leader? You will name the duties it places on leaders and see where each one shows up in a normal work week.
scope: For division and section leaders, managers and supervisors in the Disability Services Division who sign off on plans, people decisions, contracts and communications. It is not a substitute for the policy text itself, for HR or EOAD guidance, or for legal advice.
introTranscript: Welcome. This course connects the DHS Equity Policy to the plans, staffing decisions, contracts and communications leaders already manage. You will examine who is affected, what evidence is missing, which requirements apply, and what can improve. Work through the six lessons at your own pace, using the practice cases or a suitable draft within your role. Participation in this course is voluntary. The required DHS equity analysis, assigned training and other policy responsibilities remain separate. Do not enter personal case details or confidential employee information in learning reflections.

lessons.title: What the policy asks of leaders
lessons.summary: Connect the DHS Equity Policy to practical management responsibilities and the required analysis.
lessons.objective: Identify when a decision needs the formal analysis required by the DHS Equity Policy.
takeaways: The DHS Equity Policy applies to everyday work and identifies required analysis and learning responsibilities.
Leaders promote equity in strategic planning and support staff in applying an equity lens.
An optional reflection helps prepare the work; it does not certify policy compliance.
lessons.statement: A useful leadership practice connects policy expectations to a specific decision, its affected people, the evidence needed and the next responsible step.

image.caption: Examine the draft decision and the requirements that guide it.

intro.heading: Duties you can point to
intro.body:
The DHS Equity Policy asks employees to examine actions through an equity lens to reduce disparities, improve access and reduce harm. It applies to policies, practices, procedures, rules, budgets and decision-making. Management responsibilities include promoting equity in strategic planning and encouraging staff to apply an equity lens throughout daily work. Leaders help make that possible through time, resources, clear responsibilities and attention to evidence.

Consider a draft change to service-request instructions. Who will use it? Does the new step add work for small providers or people with limited access to the application? Which perspectives are missing? What will help show whether the change improved access? These questions can guide preparation without assuming that every group has the same needs or that a single meeting represents everyone.

The policy requires use of the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit. An action with prolonged or long-term impact scheduled for leadership approval must include the DHS Equity Analysis or Equity Scan, or a customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director. The course's preparation questions do not replace that analysis, assigned training, annual acknowledgements or other applicable responsibilities.

Accessibility, language access, workforce and procurement decisions also have their own requirements and authorized processes. A leader should identify which apply to the work rather than treat a general equity reflection as permission to set them aside. Use the source policy and responsible offices for actual decisions. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to the appropriate office within ADSA (Aging and Disability Services Administration).

inThisLesson: Read the leader duties under the DHS Equity Policy in plain language.
Match each duty to a decision you make in DSD, such as a plan, hire or contract.
Learn five terms the rest of the course relies on.
Sort common leader actions by which duty they serve.
lessons.keyStatement: Connect the policy to the decision, complete the required analysis where applicable, and keep a clear record of the next steps.

flashcards.back: The department policy that commits DHS to building equity into program design, decisions, hiring, community engagement and data use, and names leaders as responsible in their areas.
A specific thing the policy expects a leader to do in a real decision, such as asking who is affected before a plan locks. It can be pointed to and checked.
Fair access, opportunity and outcomes for people, which often means adjusting a process so it works for people it was not built around. Equity is not the same as treating everyone identically.

People who may benefit from or carry a decision’s burdens, including people not represented in the current discussion. Identify relevant service users, families, lead agencies, providers and staff without assuming one person speaks for a whole group.

Being able to show what you decided, who contributed, what you measured and how evidence informed the choice. Input may support an unchanged choice or an adjustment; record the reasons and limitations.

accordion.heading: Practical responsibilities to connect to policy

items.title: Decide with people
items.body: Before finalizing a policy, form or rate proposal, plan how people affected can inform it. Identify relevant service users, families, lead agencies and providers, including perspectives the familiar invitation list may miss. Record what you learned, how it informed the choice, and what remains uncertain. Include reasons when a choice remains unchanged. A useful engagement step does not establish that every policy requirement is complete.

items.title: Check help and burden
items.body: Ask who a change helps and who it costs, in time, money, travel or dignity, before it is final. Write the answer down.

items.title: Make access the default
items.body: Plain language, documents that follow Minnesota’s digital accessibility standard, interpretation and translation under the language-access rules that apply to the work, and meeting formats people can actually join.

items.title: Fair people decisions and honest data
items.body: Use job-relevant criteria and the authorized staffing process. For data, start with a question and confirm authority to use and share the information. Review group differences where definitions, counts and privacy protections support a meaningful comparison. A difference may deserve investigation but does not establish its cause.

tabs.label: In a plan
tabs.body: A draft can identify affected people, the engagement performed, potential burdens and a suitable review measure. An empty field tells you that evidence is missing from this record; it does not prove whether work happened elsewhere. Confirm the evidence and required analysis before making a conclusion about the decision.

tabs.label: In a hire
tabs.body: Use job-relevant skills, authorized selection procedures and consistent evaluation criteria. Comparable questions and documented reasons help examine fairness, but a short practice checklist cannot establish that the complete staffing process met its requirements. Coordinate changes to qualifications or assessment with HR.

tabs.label: In a contract
tabs.body: Examine whether a contract scope creates avoidable barriers while following procurement requirements. For example, clarify accessibility deliverables and language-access responsibilities with the appropriate specialists. A familiar vendor’s responsiveness is useful information but cannot substitute for authorized selection criteria.

tabs.label: In a memo
tabs.body: Plan the communication around its audience, purpose and urgency. Use plain language and accessible formats, and confirm timely language assistance under applicable requirements. A readable English memo alone does not establish that everyone affected can understand or act on it.

check.question: A section manager is about to finalize a change to how counties submit waiver service requests. Which action most directly meets a leader duty under the DHS Equity Policy?
check.correct: Before finalizing the change, examine which counties and providers may carry additional burdens, seek affected perspectives, and record how the evidence informed the draft.
wrong: Add a sentence to the memo saying that DHS is committed to equity and inclusion.
Send the change to all counties at once so no county gets it earlier than another.
Ask the equity office to review the memo after it has been sent.
check.feedbackCorrect: That is a useful part of the analysis: examine help and burden with affected people before finalizing the decision. It is not sufficient by itself; also complete the required toolkit or appropriately developed customized analysis for a decision covered by the policy.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A commitment sentence, simultaneous release or a review after the fact do not change the decision. Look for the step that changes what gets decided and who shapes it.

items.text: Invite affected lead agencies and service users to review a draft bulletin.
List who will need to travel farther under a new site plan.
Arrange timely qualified language assistance for a service notice under applicable requirements.
Ask whether a new form adds hours of work for small providers.
Hold a listening session with people who use services before a rule change.
Check a PDF with appropriate automated and manual accessibility review before posting.

lessons.next: Next, examine possible risks in the everyday decision process.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Morgan leads a policy section. A deputy asks for a two-page summary of how the section is living the DHS Equity Policy, due Friday. Morgan has a list of trainings staff completed, a statement in the section charter, and a community listening session held last year. Morgan also has three policy changes from the past quarter, two of which went out without any check on who they burdened. The team suggests leading with the trainings and the charter statement.
scenario.prompt: What should Morgan put at the center of the summary?
options: The policy changes, with evidence of the analysis and applicable requirements, missing information, and responsible improvements.
Only the training completion list and charter statement.
Only last year’s listening session, described as proof that current decisions meet the policy.
responses: This examines decisions and their records without equating one activity with complete compliance. Verify required analysis and name the follow-up needed where evidence or action is missing.
Required learning matters, but attendance and statements cannot show how each policy decision was examined. Connect them to the work and its applicable requirements.
Listening can inform later decisions. Check what was learned, how it was used and what current perspectives are missing rather than treating one event as a substitute for analysis.

lessons.transfer: Choose a practice decision or a suitable draft within your role. Which relevant responsibilities and preparation questions are already reflected in it? What evidence or next step would make the record clearer?

move.control: Within your assigned authority, you can help a decision record explain affected perspectives, possible burdens, evidence and responsible follow-through.
move.failure: Citing a policy or training record alone may leave the decision’s actual evidence and responsibilities unclear.
move.next: Choose a suitable draft or practice case, identify the relevant requirements, and note the evidence and next steps needed. Use an actual decision only within your authority.

objectives: Identify when a decision needs the formal analysis required by the DHS Equity Policy.
Distinguish management responsibilities from an optional learning exercise.
Match a policy, staffing or service decision to the requirement that guides it.

lessons.title: Check the everyday decision process
lessons.summary: Examine four possible process risks in practice DSD work without assuming their frequency or anyone’s intent.
lessons.objective: Locate an equity consideration in an everyday DSD work item.
takeaways: The duties get missed through speed, habit and delegation, not usually through objection.
Deciding before hearing affected perspectives is one possible risk to examine.
Each default has a specific moment where a leader could have changed it.
lessons.statement: Examine the timeline, invitation list, access arrangements and evidence before relying on the familiar process. Use the relevant requirements and authority to plan a response.

image.caption: Review the communication plan and when affected people can contribute.

intro.heading: Defaults, not villains
intro.body:
Everyday work decisions can miss an equity consideration even when a team is trying to meet a legitimate deadline or simplify a process. This lesson examines four possible risks in practice DSD work. It does not claim how frequently they occur or infer anyone’s motives.

One risk is deciding before inviting input. In this example, a team drafts and releases a bulletin before asking affected lead agencies whether the proposed timing will work. Another is relying only on a familiar invitation list. Responsive providers, counties or advocates may offer useful knowledge while other affected perspectives remain missing. Difficulty reaching someone does not establish that they are more affected; the team needs to examine who may face which burdens.

A third risk is postponing access arrangements until after release. The team promises accessible formats or translation later without checking whether the communication will meet the requirements that apply when people need it. A fourth is relying on a statewide average alone. Authorized, suitable data may allow an examination of differences by region or another relevant group, subject to privacy, small-group protections and comparability. A difference would not, by itself, establish its cause.

Each practice risk connects to a decision point: setting the timeline, choosing who to invite, preparing the communication or deciding what evidence to review. Leaders can examine those points within their authority, coordinate responsible offices where needed and record what is still unknown.

inThisLesson: Name four default patterns that skip a leader duty.
Find the leader moment inside each default.
Compare how a miss looks from inside the unit and from outside it.
Sort examples by the default they belong to.
lessons.keyStatement: A familiar process may leave an equity question unanswered; examine the particular steps and available evidence.

items.title: Decide, then announce
items.body: Build engagement into the timeline while the draft can still change. An invitation made early can support input; it does not guarantee participation. Check whether people received usable information and had a workable way to respond.

items.title: The familiar room
items.body: Examine the invitation list. For example, are small or rural providers and people who use services represented? Familiar contacts can contribute without representing everyone. Ask what perspectives are missing and how to seek them without imposing unpaid participation or disclosure.

items.title: Access as an afterthought
items.body: The moment is the release date. Build accessible formats and translation into the production schedule, not after it.

items.title: Data without a breakdown
items.body: Ask which comparisons would answer the work question, then confirm data authority, definitions, sufficient counts and privacy protections. A statewide average can hide differences; an unsafe or noncomparable breakdown can mislead or expose people. Name a data gap rather than inventing a result.

tabs.heading: How a miss looks from each side

tabs.label: Inside the unit
tabs.body: The bulletin went out on time, the memo was clear and leadership approved it. From inside, the process worked.

tabs.label: A lead agency
tabs.body: A county learns about a changed deadline the same week it takes effect, with no chance to say that the deadline falls during its busiest intake period.

tabs.label: A person using services
tabs.body: A notice about a service change arrives in a format they cannot read, in a language they do not use, and the first person they can ask is a case manager who also just found out.

tabs.label: A small provider
tabs.body: A small provider may need time to adjust staffing, explain instructions and test a new submission step. Learning about it only at launch can create a burden a larger organization absorbs more easily. Ask about those conditions before deciding; provider size alone does not tell you every organization’s capacity.

check.question: A DSD unit is rolling out a new provider enrollment form. The accessible version and translations are scheduled for two months after launch. Which default is this?
check.correct: Access as an afterthought, and the leader moment was the release schedule.
wrong: The familiar room, because only enrolled providers were asked for feedback.
Data without a breakdown, because the unit did not track who used the form.
Decide, then announce, because the form went out before the memo explained it.
check.feedbackCorrect: Right. Accessibility and language access are duties that belong in the production schedule, and the leader set that schedule.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Look at what was delayed: the accessible formats and translations. That points to access being treated as a later step, and the fix is in the release schedule.

items.text: The rate change is final before any county hears about it.
The same three provider groups are consulted on every policy.
The plain-language summary is promised for next quarter.
Stakeholder feedback is requested after the bulletin is published.
No small or rural provider is invited to review a change that may add reporting work.
The webinar has no captions and no recording.

lessons.next: Next, examine possible burdens and the evidence or requirements that guide a response.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Jordan supervises a team that maintains guidance for lead agencies. A legislative change means a form must be updated within six weeks. The team's plan is to revise the form, get legal review, publish it, and then collect feedback at the next quarterly meeting. Jordan notices that the plan has no consultation step before publication and no accessible-format step at all. The team says there is no time and that the quarterly meeting will catch problems.
scenario.prompt: What is the most useful thing Jordan can do with the plan?
options: Accept the plan, since the legislative deadline is real and feedback will come at the quarterly meeting.
Push the publication date back by a month to allow full consultation, and ask legal whether the deadline can move.

Plan a targeted review with affected lead agencies during the available window, coordinate accessible formats and applicable language access, and confirm the required analysis and authorized release steps.
responses: A statutory deadline matters, but it does not automatically remove engagement, accessibility or analysis responsibilities. Ask the responsible offices how to meet applicable requirements within the available time.
Do not assume a date can or cannot move. An authorized review should examine the requirement, available alternatives and effects of delay rather than promise a universal extension.

Targeted engagement can strengthen a draft within limited time. Its sufficiency must be assessed with the other applicable requirements; consulting a few agencies is not automatic proof that every duty is met.

lessons.transfer: Choose a practice case or suitable draft. Which possible process risk deserves investigation, and which timeline, invitation or evidence question would help?

move.control: Within your authority, you can examine timelines, invitation lists, access arrangements and evidence, and coordinate the responsible review where needed.
move.failure: An unexamined process may leave affected perspectives or access needs out of the decision; check the actual steps before drawing that conclusion.
move.next: For optional practice, review a practice timeline or suitable draft and propose a relevant contribution or access step with a responsible person. Choose a useful review point for the learning activity.

objectives: Locate an equity consideration in an everyday DSD work item.
Explain how a routine default can change who can use a service or opportunity.
Identify evidence needed to review whether an equity-plan action improved practice.

lessons.title: Examine possible process burdens
lessons.summary: Examine who may carry a process burden and what evidence or requirement should guide the response.
lessons.objective: Identify people who may carry a decision’s burdens.
takeaways: A process change may create unequal burdens; seek evidence and affected perspectives.
Equity analysis works alongside applicable accessibility, language-access and workplace requirements.
A record of the review helps explain a decision without certifying every duty or proving cause.
lessons.statement: Identify a possible burden, examine the supporting account and use the relevant requirements to choose a responsible response. A process gap does not by itself establish who was affected or guarantee that one repair prevents recurrence.

image.caption: Colleagues sit around a table with papers and notebooks during a meeting.

intro.heading: The cost has an address
intro.body:
A process change can create different burdens for different people. A tighter deadline may require a small provider to reorganize work. A notice in an unusable format may prevent someone from understanding a service change. Those possibilities deserve examination rather than an assumption that every small provider or language group has the same experience. Seek the affected perspectives and evidence needed to understand the situation.

The DHS Equity Policy works alongside other requirements. Minnesota’s digital accessibility standard adopts WCAG 2.1 levels A and AA and qualified Section 508 requirements for covered technology, with specified applicability and exceptions. Public entities also have effective-communication responsibilities under ADA Title II. In health programs and activities covered by 45 CFR 92.201, language assistance required for meaningful access must be accurate, timely, free of charge and protective of privacy and independent decision-making. Confirm the applicable scope with the responsible offices; one general course cannot decide the legal requirements of a particular release.

A useful record connects an observed barrier, its evidence, the requirement or practical concern involved, the response and the person responsible. For example, a notice can be reviewed for accessibility and language access before release, then checked for whether recipients could use it. A record of that review helps explain the decision. It does not certify every duty or prove that the change caused all later results.

inThisLesson: Trace where the cost of a missed duty lands in three DSD examples.
Connect each leader duty to the law or policy that already backs it.
Recognize what good practice looks like in the record.
Sort statements by whether they describe cost, backing or good practice.
lessons.keyStatement: Name the observed barrier, its evidence and the responsible next step.

items.title: Accessibility
items.body: For covered technology, use the Minnesota digital accessibility standard and appropriate specialist review. An automated checker can identify some issues, but it cannot establish full usability or compliance. Confirm the applicable requirements, review manually where needed and coordinate effective communication or accommodation through the proper process.

items.title: Language access
items.body: For health programs and activities covered by 45 CFR 92.201, required language assistance must be accurate, timely, free of charge and protect privacy and independent decision-making. Required interpretation uses a qualified interpreter and required translation a qualified translator. Ask the authorized language-access process what is needed for the particular communication; a later translation promise alone does not establish meaningful access now.

items.title: Workplace responsibilities
items.body: Use the policy that fits the concern. MMB Policy 1432 covers disrespectful conduct outside protected-class concerns and sexual harassment. Policy 1436 covers protected-class harassment and discrimination, with immediate manager reporting to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Accommodation requests follow Policy 1433. These processes serve different purposes and are not replaced by a team equity discussion.

items.title: Evidence and data
items.body: A group difference can help identify a question for further review when the data is authorized, comparable and suitable for the purpose. Check definitions, missing information and small-group exposure. Describe what the figures show without assigning a cause or publishing protected data merely because the report has removed names.

tabs.label: A deadline
tabs.body: A reporting deadline moved up by two weeks is absorbed by a large agency. A two-person rural provider misses it, and the consequence is a compliance finding, not a conversation.

tabs.label: A notice
tabs.body: In a practice case, an English-only service notice may not be usable for a family that needs language assistance. An informal explanation may miss important details. The team should coordinate qualified assistance through the applicable process rather than assume an informal translation meets the requirements.

tabs.label: A hire
tabs.body: A supervisor hires a familiar internal candidate without a consistent process. The decision may be fine, but it cannot be explained, and the candidates who were not favored learn that the process was not for them.

check.question: A service notice affects people eligible for a health program covered by 45 CFR 92.201. A colleague suggests publishing in English now and treating later translation as sufficient. What should the leader do?
check.correct: Use the authorized language-access process to confirm and arrange timely meaningful access under the applicable requirements before assuming the release is adequate.
wrong: Assume a promise to translate later always meets the requirement.
Require each person to supply and pay for an interpreter.
Use an English plain-language summary as proof that language access is complete.
check.feedbackCorrect: Meaningful access depends on the communication and requirements, not a universal waiting period. Required assistance must be timely, accurate and free of charge. The authorized review should establish how people can understand and act on the notice when needed.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A later promise, a self-supplied interpreter or an English summary cannot establish meaningful access. Identify the audience and importance of the notice, and coordinate the appropriate qualified assistance through the applicable process.

items.text: A rural provider misses a deadline it never had a chance to comment on.
Applicable language-access rules require timely meaningful access.
The consultation log records who contributed, when, and how input informed the decision, including unchanged choices and their reasons.
A person using a screen reader cannot open the notice.
The report uses authorized group comparisons with suitable counts and clear limitations.
The ADA requires public programs to be accessible to people with disabilities.

lessons.next: Next, use six preparation questions to identify evidence and follow-up for a practice case or suitable draft. These questions do not replace the required analysis.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Avery manages a contracts unit. A grant program for community organizations was announced with a three-week application window, an online-only form, and instructions in English. Two weeks in, an organization serving Hmong families writes that they cannot complete the form in time and ask for help. A colleague suggests treating it as a one-off and offering an extension to that organization only. Another suggests reopening the window for everyone, which the program lead says would delay awards by a month.
scenario.prompt: How should Avery think about this?
options: Offer the one organization a quiet extension and move on, since the window was published and most applicants managed.
Treat it as a signal that the design missed a duty: name who else likely could not apply, fix the access gap for this round in a way that is fair to all, and change the template for next round.
Decline the extension to keep the process consistent and invite the organization to apply next year.
responses: A quiet exception helps one applicant and hides the pattern. The organizations that did not write in are still excluded, and the next round repeats the miss.

Treat the letter as a reason to examine the design and who else may face a barrier. Coordinate a fair response with the authorized grant and language-access offices; do not personally waive deadlines, terms or other requirements. Record the evidence, response and remaining limitations.
Consistency in an inaccessible process is consistent exclusion. The duty is to make access the default, not to apply the barrier evenly.

lessons.transfer: Use a practice case or suitable past decision without identifying anyone. What possible burden was observed, what supports it and what remains unknown?

move.control: Within your role, you can identify affected perspectives, possible burdens and access arrangements for the responsible review.
move.failure: A concern may remain unexamined when there is no appropriate account or follow-up. Silence does not establish that a burden exists or that none exists.
move.next: For optional practice, add appropriate notes about affected perspectives, possible burdens and access arrangements to a practice case or suitable draft. If useful, discuss the notes with your team and choose a review point within your role.

objectives: Identify people who may carry a decision’s burdens.
Connect an accessibility or language-access concern to its supporting requirement.
Name a missing perspective and a practical way to seek it before deciding.

lessons.title: The six-line check
lessons.summary: Six reflection questions help prepare an equity review; the required analysis remains a separate policy responsibility.
lessons.objective: Record specific answers to the six preparation questions on a sample draft.
takeaways: The six questions are an optional preparation method, not the DHS Equity Analysis Toolkit or a claim of compliance.
An honest 'not yet' is more useful than a vague 'yes'.
The check works on plans, hires, contracts and memos alike.
lessons.statement: Use the six questions to prepare a clear record of evidence and unresolved issues. Carry the relevant information into the actual required analysis and responsible review.

image.caption: A short reflection can reveal questions to carry into the required equity analysis.

intro.heading: Six lines before it locks
intro.body:
These six reflection questions help you prepare a draft for equity review. They do not, by themselves, fulfill DHS’s analysis requirements. For covered actions, complete the DHS Equity Analysis or Equity Scan, or a customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director. Here they are. One: who is affected, including people not in the room. Two: who has contributed, and how the input informed the choice, including reasons for an unchanged choice. Three: who is burdened, and what we did about it. Four: what access steps are done, meaning plain language, accessible format, translation and interpretation where needed. Five: which formal processes apply, such as procurement, HR, accommodation or data privacy, and what responsible next steps are needed. Six: what we will measure using authorized and suitable data, and when we will look.

Run it on the draft, not the final. Write the answers on the document or in the file. If a line says 'not yet', that is useful. It tells you what to do before the decision goes out, or it tells the approver what was skipped and why. A 'yes' without supporting information needs clarification. A blank row shows that this record is incomplete; check what happened before concluding a requirement was missed.

Allow enough time to examine evidence, hear affected perspectives and complete the required analysis; a short reflection does not set the time needed for a sound review. It is the same six lines for a position description, a contract scope or a team work plan. The next lesson handles the harder cases and applicable formal processes. This lesson is about getting the routine into your hands.

inThisLesson: Learn the six lines and what a good answer to each looks like.
Practice filling the lines on a sample DSD bulletin.
See how the answers travel with the decision to the approver.
Sort example answers by whether they are usable, vague or missing.
lessons.keyStatement: Use six questions to prepare; use the required tool and process to complete the formal analysis.

accordion.heading: What a good answer looks like

items.title: Who is affected
items.body: Identify the relevant groups and workplace practices without unnecessary personal details. For example, examine lead agencies in a region, small providers facing a reporting step and people who use the service. Do not assume a named group is homogeneous or that one contact represents every affected person.

items.title: Who contributed and how input informed the choice
items.body: Record the relevant participants or groups, dates, what was learned and how it informed the decision. Input may support an existing choice, prompt an adjustment or identify an unresolved question. Explain the reasons for unchanged choices rather than invent a change.

items.title: Who is burdened and what we did
items.body: Identify who may carry a burden and the supporting evidence, including uncertainty. Describe an adjustment considered, such as a longer window, phone option, simpler form or funded transition. Check decision authority and applicable requirements before treating an option as available.

items.title: What we will measure
items.body: Choose an indicator connected to the question and identify its definition, source, review date and owner. Examine group comparisons only where authorized use, privacy protections, counts and comparability support them. Missing evidence stays unknown; a recorded difference is a question to examine, not a demonstrated cause.

tabs.label: A bulletin
tabs.body: Practice provider-bulletin example: identify which lead agencies, providers and service users are affected by the particular change rather than assume every organization is affected equally. Small providers may face an additional reporting burden; investigate their actual capacity. Prepare accessible communication and any required language assistance for the time it is needed. One possible review question is whether on-time submission rates differ by provider size after ninety days. Before using that indicator, obtain authorized data review, confirm definitions and comparable counts, protect small groups and avoid inferring cause from a difference. The period and indicator are practice choices, not official standards.

tabs.label: A position description
tabs.body: Practice hiring example: identify which internal and external candidates a position description may affect. Examine whether a degree requirement is necessary for the actual work and how it may exclude experienced candidates without that credential. Use authorized HR classification and selection procedures. Possible evidence includes the applicant pool and panel ratings, reviewed with HR for authorized use, comparability and privacy; these figures alone do not establish why a difference occurred.

tabs.label: A contract scope
tabs.body: Practice grant example: identify the community organizations and service users affected by the proposed scope. Examine whether its cash-flow arrangements could burden smaller organizations; organization size alone does not establish financial capacity. Coordinate procurement review of permissible payment arrangements rather than promise advance payment. Prepare a clear, accessible application and any required language assistance. Record evidence, authorized options and unresolved questions.

check.question: A supervisor fills in line two of the check on a draft policy as 'Stakeholders consulted: yes.' What is the most useful next step?
check.correct: Ask who contributed, when, what was learned and how it informed the choice, including reasons for an unchanged choice; record missing information for follow-up.
wrong: Accept the line, since the supervisor is closer to the work and knows who was consulted.
Replace the line with a note that consultation will happen at the next quarterly meeting.
Remove line two for this policy because the timeline is short.
check.feedbackCorrect: Names or groups, dates and a clear account of what was learned make the note useful. Input may change a draft or support an existing choice; record either honestly. Missing details mean this note needs follow-up, not automatic proof that no engagement occurred.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A general yes does not provide enough evidence to review the work. Ask who participated, when, what was learned and how it informed the decision. If the information is unavailable, record that limitation and seek the appropriate follow-up rather than assert that a blank row proves noncompliance.

items.text: Consulted: three northwest lead agencies on 4 March; extended the window by two weeks as a result.
Burden: minimal.
Access: see communications team.
Possible practice measure: compare on-time submissions by provider size after ninety days, subject to authorized data review, comparable counts and privacy protections.
Who is affected: all stakeholders.
Applicable formal processes and responsible offices: not yet considered.

lessons.next: Next, examine difficult choices and the concerns that require a formal process or responsible office.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Sam is a new section manager and wants to introduce the six-line check. The section has four policy analysts, each with a different style. One analyst already does something like it informally and worries that writing it down will slow everything. Another thinks the check should be a separate form routed to the equity office. The section's next three deliverables are due within a month. Sam has about thirty minutes at the next staff meeting. The deliverables with long-term impact will also need the analysis required by the DHS Equity Policy.
scenario.prompt: What is the best way for Sam to introduce the check?
options: Practice the six questions on one live draft, keep the notes with it, and identify the required toolkit or appropriately developed customized analysis for each covered deliverable.
Build a separate form, route it to the equity office for review, and make it a required attachment for all policy products.
Share the six lines by email and ask analysts to use them when they have time, since the deliverables are tight.
responses: This builds a useful preparation habit while keeping the formal analysis requirement visible. Notes inform the required analysis rather than replacing it.

Do not invent a substitute mandatory form. Staff remain responsible for their work, and the policy requires the toolkit or a customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director where applicable.
The reflection is optional learning support. Required analysis cannot be skipped because a deadline is tight; plan time for the applicable process.

lessons.transfer: Choose a practice case or suitable draft within your role. Which preparation questions can you answer with evidence, and which need further information or authorized review?

move.control: You can identify preparation gaps honestly and carry out the applicable analysis responsibilities assigned to your role.
move.failure: A preparation note may look complete while its evidence or responsible next steps remain unclear.
move.next: Try the preparation questions with a practice case or suitable draft. Record how evidence informed the choice, whether it changed or remained the same, and identify any responsible follow-up.

objectives: Record specific answers to the six preparation questions on a sample draft.
Distinguish usable evidence from a vague assurance that a review occurred.
Identify the required analysis that must accompany a covered action.

lessons.title: Hard calls and formal responsibilities
lessons.summary: Distinguish decisions within your authority from concerns that require a formal process or responsible office.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an improvement within your authority from a concern requiring a formal process.
takeaways: Identify the applicable process before trying to resolve a sensitive concern.
Protected-class concerns, accommodation requests, data privacy and procurement have distinct responsibilities.
A recorded trade-off supports review; it does not authorize disregarding a requirement.
lessons.statement: Check the applicable process and assigned responsibilities before responding to a sensitive concern. Use the responsible office promptly and act within your authority.

image.caption: Papers are arranged for review. Preparation questions support the review; formal responsibilities still apply.

intro.heading: Decide what is yours; refer what is not
intro.body:
A leader can improve workplace practices while respecting the responsibilities of other offices. A concern about protected-class harassment or discrimination belongs under MMB Policy 1436 and the agency’s complaint procedures. Managers and supervisors must immediately report allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Do not replace this with a private warning, require further incidents before reporting, or promise secrecy that the process cannot guarantee.

Authorized investigations follow the agency’s investigation procedures. This course does not prohibit a manager from performing an assigned role under those procedures; it discourages improvised fact-finding or settlement outside them. Policy 1432 has a separate scope for disrespectful behavior that does not involve protected-class status or sexual harassment. Informal resolution may be appropriate when possible, but is not a prerequisite to a formal complaint.

A disability accommodation request follows Policy 1433. Promptly forward the request to the appropriate decision maker and notify the ADA Coordinator. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation; any appropriate request belongs to the ADA Coordinator. A procurement, grant, eligibility or licensing decision also needs its authorized process.

If a safety or possible maltreatment concern arises, use applicable immediate-help and reporting procedures. Reporting duties depend on the role, circumstances and governing requirements; this course does not designate every learner a mandated reporter. Do not delay a reporting duty that applies while discussing an equity reflection.

For choices within your authority, record the options, evidence, burdens and reason for the decision. When requirements conflict or a deadline appears impossible, seek authorized guidance rather than create a personal exception. Keep the unresolved question and responsible follow-up visible.

inThisLesson: Identify applicable formal processes and responsible offices.
Distinguish a choice within delegated authority from a formal referral in DSD practice cases.
Learn how to decide and record a trade-off when the six lines conflict.
Sort situations into decide, refer, or both.
lessons.keyStatement: Use the appropriate process promptly, and act within the responsibilities assigned to you.

items.title: HR, EOAD and accommodation
items.body: For allegations or incidents of protected-class harassment or discrimination, managers immediately report to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436. Follow assigned complaint and investigation procedures rather than settle the matter privately. Accommodation requests follow Policy 1433, including its limits on supervisors requesting medical information. Ordinary respectful-workplace concerns have Policy 1432’s separate process.

items.title: Maltreatment reporting and legal
items.body: Know the reporting requirements that apply to your role and the situation. For vulnerable adults, section 626.557 distinguishes mandated reporting responsibilities and voluntary reports; actual duties require the applicable definitions and procedures. Do not delay a duty that applies while seeking routine learning advice. Legal exposure, data privacy and statutory interpretation require the appropriate authorized review.

items.title: Procurement, eligibility and licensing
items.body: Contract and grant awards follow procurement rules. Individual eligibility determinations and 245D licensing actions belong to the offices with that authority.

tabs.label: Name the trade-off
tabs.body: Describe the options and the requirement in tension. For example, an available review window may reach only a few lead agencies. Record whose perspectives remain missing and what consequences may follow. A limited invitation list is evidence of the current process, not proof that all affected perspectives have been represented.

tabs.label: Decide and say why
tabs.body: Decide within your authority after checking applicable requirements. A written reason should explain the evidence, alternatives and limitations rather than serve as an exception to a requirement. If authority or compliance is unresolved, obtain the responsible office’s guidance and record the next step.

tabs.label: Set the look-back
tabs.body: Name the review question, date and responsible person. Use authorized evidence to examine intended results and possible burdens, with suitable privacy and small-group protections. Review may identify a need to adjust the decision; it cannot retroactively excuse a requirement that applied at release.

check.question: A staff member tells a supervisor that a colleague has made repeated comments about their accent and asks the supervisor to 'just handle it quietly.' What should the supervisor do?
check.correct: Listen, explain the applicable reporting responsibility, immediately report the allegation to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436, and follow agency procedures.
wrong: Have a private word with the colleague and check back in a month, since the staff member asked for discretion.
Hold a team meeting on respectful communication without naming anyone.
Ask the staff member to document further incidents before deciding whether to escalate.
check.feedbackCorrect: Comments about an accent may raise a national-origin concern. Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Keep support respectful and explain confidentiality limits; authorized review determines the facts and response.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A private warning or a general meeting does not replace immediate manager reporting under Policy 1436. Do not wait for more incidents or treat this as an ordinary Policy 1432 disagreement. Report to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer and follow the agency’s complaint and investigation procedures without promising an outcome.

items.text: Whether to extend a comment window within delegated authority and applicable requirements.
A staff member requests a schedule change because of a disability.
A grant scope may create access barriers, and changes to its award terms require authorized procurement review.
Which lead agencies to invite first within delegated authority, while checking applicable engagement requirements and missing perspectives.
A possible maltreatment concern needs the reporting route and requirements applicable to your role.
Choosing a grant scope that small organizations can apply for, with awards under procurement rules.

lessons.next: Finally, apply the preparation questions to a practice case or suitable draft and plan the responsible next steps.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Riley directs a section developing provider-rate guidance. A proposal has a statutory submission date in five weeks. Small rural providers report a possible additional reporting burden. Available figures do not yet support a reliable regional comparison. The team suggests recording the concern but treating the deadline as permission to skip the required equity analysis.
options: Treat the deadline as a waiver and describe the unresolved burden as a completed analysis.
Coordinate the required analysis and authorized guidance on timing, examine available affected perspectives, and record the burden, data gap and responsible next steps.
Promise a later submission without checking the statutory requirement or decision authority.
responses: A deadline does not automatically waive required analysis. Describing an unresolved concern as a finished review conceals the evidence gap rather than resolving it.

This keeps the actual requirement visible and uses the responsible offices to address timing. The record should distinguish evidence gathered, unresolved questions and next actions; a look-back date is not a substitute for obligations that apply before submission.
A delay may have consequences and needs authorized review. Do not promise an extension or assume there is no workable alternative without checking the requirement and available options.

lessons.transfer: Consider a practice situation or a suitable past decision without identifying anyone. What signal would indicate a required formal process or responsible office, and what would your assigned next step be?

move.control: You can help your team identify responsible offices, use applicable processes promptly and document choices within its authority.
move.failure: An improvised response may delay a required process or leave a concern without the appropriate review.
move.next: Check your team’s current contact routes and applicable procedures with the responsible offices. Use the practice case to practice when and how to refer a concern.

objectives: Distinguish an improvement within your authority from a concern requiring a formal process.
Route a protected-class concern immediately and follow the agency’s assigned complaint and investigation procedures.
Document a trade-off without presenting it as permission to disregard a requirement.

lessons.title: Practice the review and plan responsible next steps
lessons.summary: Use a practice case or suitable draft to identify evidence, a supported improvement and responsible next steps.
lessons.objective: Apply the preparation questions to a practice case or suitable draft and identify a supported improvement or unresolved question.
takeaways: One live decision done well teaches more than a dozen examples.
Repair means naming what was missed and changing the decision or the next step, not apologizing in a memo.
The review is where the practice becomes a habit: what changed, what did not, what to do next time.
lessons.statement: Practice with a practice case or suitable draft, distinguish evidence from unresolved questions and identify responsible next steps. The exercise does not require a live decision or certify completion of its duties.

image.caption: A draft can be examined for evidence, unresolved questions and responsible next steps.

intro.heading: Pick the object; run the check; repair
intro.body:
Choose the practice case or a suitable draft within your role. A bulletin, a policy draft, a position description, a contract scope, a team work plan, a data report. Run the six lines on it and write the answers on the draft. Who is affected. Who contributed and how input informed the choice, including reasons for unchanged choices. Who is burdened and what we did. What access steps are done. Which formal processes apply and what responsible next steps are needed. What we will measure using authorized, suitable evidence, and when.

Some lines will come back 'not yet'. That is the repair list. For each one, decide: change the decision, add a step before it goes out, or obtain the authorized guidance needed to resolve a requirement or timing conflict and record the follow-up. Use an applicable formal process promptly. Repair is not a paragraph of regret in the cover memo. It is a change to what goes out or to what happens next.

Then review. Sit with a peer or your supervisor for fifteen minutes and answer three questions. What changed in the decision because of the check? What did not change and why? What will you do differently on the next one? Write the answers down. That review is the moment the course becomes a practice, and it is also the start of the next course in this pathway, which builds equity into team goals so the check is no longer a solo act.

For actual decisions covered by the DHS Equity Policy, identify and follow the required equity-analysis process. These reflections support preparation and follow-through; they do not certify that the required analysis or other duties have been completed.

inThisLesson: Choose the practice case or a suitable draft within your role.
Use the preparation questions and distinguish known evidence from missing information.
Identify a supported improvement or authorized next step.
Plan a review with a peer or supervisor where useful; actual work completion is not required for the learning exercise.
lessons.keyStatement: Practice on a suitable draft or practice case, and identify the evidence and responsible actions needed.

items.title: Change the decision
items.body: The burden line showed a small-provider cost, so the reporting window is extended or a phone option is added before release.

items.title: Add a step
items.body: The access line was 'not yet', so the accessible version and the translation move onto the release date and a named person owns them.

items.title: Use the process
items.body: A staff concern may involve national origin, so the manager immediately reports it under Policy 1436 and follows agency procedures. A team communication exercise can support better practice, but it cannot replace a reporting responsibility or authorized investigation.

items.title: Record the trade-off
items.body: A statutory date and unresolved language-access issue need authorized review. Record the actual constraint, alternatives considered, responsible guidance and remaining actions. A later review can examine results; it does not by itself authorize a release that fails applicable requirements.

tabs.label: What changed
tabs.body: Name the concrete differences in the decision: a window, a format, a consultation, a measure. If the answer is nothing, say so plainly.

tabs.label: What did not
tabs.body: Name unresolved questions and why they remain: missing evidence, an authority decision or an unfinished access step. Explain how they will be addressed through the appropriate process. The record should distinguish a practical limitation from a requirement that must be met, rather than use a deadline as a blanket excuse.

tabs.label: Next time
tabs.body: Pick one thing to do earlier on the next decision, such as putting consultation on the timeline before the date is set.

check.question: A provider bulletin includes important information for people eligible for a covered health program. Translations are not ready, and the team proposes an English-first release followed by translation three weeks later. What is the most responsible next step?
check.correct: Coordinate authorized language-access and release review to arrange timely meaningful access under applicable requirements, rather than assume delayed translations and interim interpretation are automatically sufficient.
wrong: Release in English because any later translation date satisfies meaningful access.
Treat an English plain-language summary as a substitute for every language-access need.
Mention the delay only in the next quarterly report.
check.feedbackCorrect: The importance, audience and timing of the communication matter. Required assistance in covered health programs must be accurate, timely and free of charge. An authorized review should establish a workable release approach and qualified assistance; this course cannot universally approve a three-week gap.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A later promise, English summary or quarterly explanation cannot establish timely meaningful access. Identify the applicable requirements and affected recipients, and coordinate the authorized language-access and release decision before assuming the gap is acceptable.

items.text: Writing who is affected on the draft bulletin.
Moving the accessible version onto the release date with an owner.
Telling a peer what changed and what did not.
Immediately reporting a protected-class concern through the applicable agency process.
Recording which formal processes apply, or explaining why none identified applies after appropriate review.
Choosing one thing to do earlier next time.

lessons.next: Use the job aid when it helps you prepare a draft or practice review. Continue related learning at your own pace; required work procedures remain separate.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Casey leads a data and evaluation unit. A quarterly waiver-access report shows statewide averages. The team proposes regional and race comparisons, but has not yet checked authorized use and sharing, group definitions, missing information or small counts. The report is due in four days. An analyst suggests leaving all comparisons out because they might prompt questions.
options: Omit the comparisons only because they could raise difficult questions.
Publish every proposed breakdown because removing names always makes it safe.
Obtain authorized data and privacy review, include supported comparisons with suitable protections and limitations, and explain evidence that remains unavailable.
responses: Potentially uncomfortable findings deserve careful review, not automatic omission. Check whether the comparison is meaningful and authorized, then explain the findings and limits.
Removing names does not guarantee safe disclosure. Small counts and combinations of details may expose people, and different definitions or missing records can make comparisons misleading.

This examines both useful evidence and its limits. Confirm authority, comparability and protections before sharing. Describe differences without claiming cause, and do not treat this report as proof that the required equity analysis or every duty is complete.

lessons.transfer: Use the practice case or a suitable draft within your role. What evidence, responsible next step and review question would make the preparation useful?

move.control: You can choose an appropriate practice case, prepare a supported account and identify next actions within your role.
move.failure: Saving a job aid alone does not establish that a preparation question, required analysis or follow-through action was completed.
move.next: Use the practice case or a suitable draft within your authority. Record a supported improvement or unresolved question, the responsible next step and a review date. Actual work need not be completed to finish the learning exercise.

objectives: Apply the preparation questions to a practice case or suitable draft and identify a supported improvement or unresolved question.
Recognize when required equity analysis applies and identify the responsible next steps.
Record a responsible person, follow-through action and suitable review date without certifying completion.

jobAid.subtitle: Identify the issue. Hear affected perspectives. Check requirements. Use the responsible process. Review evidence. Plan follow-through.
remember: Use the source policy to identify responsibilities that apply to the work.
Use the six questions to prepare, not to replace required DHS equity analysis.
Follow the appropriate authorized process for sensitive concerns and decisions.

sections.heading: Before the decision locks
items: Write who is affected, by name of group, including people not in the room.
Describe who contributed, when, and how input informed the decision, including unchanged choices and their reasons.
Identify who may carry a burden, what evidence supports that concern and what response or further review is needed.
Confirm plain language, accessible format, translation and interpretation are on the release date.
For a covered action, complete the DHS Equity Analysis or Equity Scan, or a customized tool developed in consultation with an equity director.

sections.heading: Check formal processes and responsible offices
items: Protected-class harassment or discrimination: managers immediately report to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436 and follow agency procedures.
Respectful workplace concerns outside protected-class status or sexual harassment: follow Policy 1432 and agency procedures.
Accommodation requests: promptly forward through the appropriate process; supervisors do not request medical information or documentation.
Safety and possible maltreatment: follow immediate-help and reporting requirements applicable to the role and situation.
Contracts, eligibility, licensing, legal and data privacy: coordinate with the office that has the relevant authority.

sections.heading: When the lines conflict
items: Name the options, evidence and actual constraint.
Decide within your authority and complete applicable requirements; obtain authorized guidance for an unresolved conflict.
Record the next action, responsible person and review date.

sections.heading: Measure and look back
items: Choose a measure that answers the question, with clear definitions and authorized use.
Confirm privacy, suitable counts and comparability before sharing group results.
Describe observed differences without claiming cause, and record missing evidence and follow-up.

sections.heading: Repair and review
items: Turn an unresolved question into a supported change, an authorized review or a responsible follow-up; do not use it as permission to disregard a requirement.
Hold a fifteen-minute review: what changed, what did not, what to do earlier next time.
Keep the answers with the decision so the next person can see them.
